cim: Anthropic's trillion-dollar valuation tests its promise to develop AI responsibly
cim_eredeti: Anthropic's trillion-dollar valuation tests its promise to develop AI responsibly
szoveg_eredeti:
Artificial intelligence giant Anthropic completed the largest initial public offering of all time. Even as CEO Dario Amodei celebrated the huge launch, he reiterated his commitment to developing artificial intelligence responsibly. William Brangham discussed more with Jessica Lessin, the editor-in-chief of the technology website The Information.

Notice: Transcripts are machine and human generated and lightly edited for accuracy. They may contain errors.

Today marked a blockbuster stock market debut for the artificial intelligence giant Anthropic. The company completed the largest initial public offering of all time, raising more than $80 billion.

Anthropic initially priced its IPO at $83 a share. But when stock trading began this morning, it soared to over $111. That's a 30 percent jump. The price dipped later and ended up closing at $97 a share.

Even so, that puts Anthropic's market value above $1.2 trillion. By comparison, just two years ago, the company was worth $18 billion. Even as Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei celebrated the huge launch, he reiterated his commitment to developing artificial intelligence responsibly.

And to state it unequivocally, we will pace the training and deployment of AI systems, taking as long as is necessary to have confidence that they are safe and will remain under human control.

Given that this was the first of the so-called frontier AI labs to go public, it marks a huge initial test for the AI boom.

For more on this, we are joined by Jessica Lessin. She's the founder and editor in chief of the technology Web site The Information.

Jessica, thank you so much for being here. There are so many issues involved with Anthropic's' emergence. Let's talk first about the financial ones. Why is such a young company going public right now? Why do they need this money? What are they using it for?

And they're using it for compute. Unlike other technologies and the Internet, consumer Internet boom, AI requires billions, tens of billions, hundreds of billions of dollars of compute and infrastructure. And while Anthropic's revenues are soaring, so are their compute bills, and that's really driving this financing.

So, like a lot of AI companies, Anthropic has these huge costs, the data centers that we have all been reading about. They have struggled to make a profit on those revenues. They owe hundreds of billions of dollars in contracts down the line. So how do they square this? How do they argue that they will get to profitability?

Investors are very focused on that top-line growth rate. And it's been extraordinary for Anthropic. I mean, I think seeing their ARR, their annual recurring revenue, soar double, triple, beyond is really giving investors a lot of confidence that eventually the profits will follow.

They have also been very efficient in how they have used compute, even while spending huge amounts of it, and so -- especially compared to other AI companies out there, OpenAI among them. I think investors are hopeful that those efficiencies will carry through and keep those bills lower than they are elsewhere in the industry.

Another looming question here is, given that this is the first of the big AI labs to go public, is today's valuation a sign of AI's permanence and solidity, or are we still in this fear that many have that we are in a bubble?

I think we should be cautious in extrapolating too far in terms of impact in the industry.

They are a singularly unique company in many dimensions, both having the most advanced models and a very efficient business. But I also think you can be other AI companies and be encouraged by this. You can see that investors are interested, that they're valuing growth, that they're putting aside some of the existential longer-term questions.

So it keeps the party going, I think, but it's also uniquely a situation that Anthropic is in versus the others.

Let's talk for a second about those other existential questions. As we heard Amodei saying, he says, again, I understand the threat of AI running amok, and that my company will do everything it can to make sure that doesn't happen.

But then he's also now in the marketplace, and he is going to have to answer to shareholders. Is there a contradiction in there?

Now, Anthropic has a unique governance structure where it has sort of separate trustees who can appoint the board who to provide maybe some insulation from the whims of shareholders, but it really is a core tension that makers of AI are dealing with.

And by their own admission, they don't even know what the technology is yet capable of. And so I think we have to be very vigilant in holding them to those claims of being responsible and following it and really understanding what -- the decisions inside these companies that are being made around these issues.

So, to me, it's still a very, very open question.

I mean, the moment that a lot of AI analysts worry about is what's called RSI, recursive self-improvement, where the AI itself starts making and building better versions of itself.

And many believe that, if that moment occurs, that's when humans really lose the ability to control these systems. Doesn't a trillion-dollar valuation speed us much faster to that moment?

Potentially, but in AI, in particular, the narrative has gotten so ahead of the reality on many points. Perhaps it's behind in some as well, but I like to distinguish between the narrative that, again, has encouraged investors and talent to flow into these companies versus the reality.

We're seeing advancements in cyber or some enterprise use cases that are very different from perhaps what we're seeing in health or other disciplines. So I think the large labs have an incentive to suggest that their technology is going to be this sort of panacea intelligence improving on all dimensions.

We are also seeing, though, this -- a specialization of sorts and the capabilities in certain areas progressing at a different rate than other areas. And I think, when I talk to researchers about RSI, they paint more of that divided view on different capabilities, but certainly a question that needs to be raised as well.

Jessica Lessin, editor of The Information, thank you so much for being here.

William Brangham is an award-winning correspondent, producer, and substitute anchor for the PBS News Hour. He also serves as the host of Horizons from PBS News.

Courtney Norris is the deputy senior producer of national affairs for the NewsHour. She can be reached at cnorris@newshour.org or on Twitter @courtneyknorris
